newsitem.title: USA: Clinton to open new season of cooperation.
newsitem.headline: Clinton to open new season of cooperation.

text.p: President Bill Clinton hoped to usher in a new season of bipartisan cooperation with an inaugural speech designed to "help flush the poison from the atmosphere," The Washington Post reported on Sunday.

In an interview with the newspaper, Clinton said the "big fights" with Republicans over the role of government during his first term were largely settled in his favour, clearing the way for consensus.
Clinton also urged that ethics controversies at the White House and on Capitol Hill be settled as quickly as possible so that the country could move on.
"We spend in general a disproportionate amount of time on all this kind of stuff and it takes not only time, but it takes enormous emotional energy away from the work of the country," he said.
He pleaded with people to "look at the evidence and just make whatever judgments they think they have to make and put it behind us."
Clinton will take the oath of office on Monday for a second term and then deliver an inaugural address laying out his hopes and plans for the next four years.

"I hope that I can set a tone on Monday and in the days ahead that will help flush the poison out of the atmosphere and get people to thinking about the folks that sent us all here," he said in the interview.
Clinton told the Post he expected to forge bipartisan agreements to eliminate the budget deficit and "make the adjustments necessary to preserve Social Security and Medicare for future generations."
He also said he would be outspoken in public appearances and grassroots lobbying to enact changes in campaign finance laws and to defeat a proposed balanced budget amendment to the Constitution.

In his first public defence of his use of the White House to entertain political supporters, Clinton asserted in the interview he had every right to invite generous contributors for overnight stays, the Post said.

"I do not think it is a bad thing for a president to invite his strong supporters to stay in the White House. I think it would be a bad thing for anyone to be told if you give such and such amount of money, we'll let you spend the night in the Lincoln Bedroom," he said.
"But I can tell you, that did not happen. That just did not happen," Clinton added.
A Washington Post-ABC News poll published with the interview showed Clinton beginning his second term more popular with Americans than at any time since the early days of his presidency.

The survey of 1,206 adults conducted Jan. 13-15 found that 60 percent of those interviewed approved of the way Clinton was handling his job as president. The poll has a margin of error of plus or minus three percentage points.
